quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on cut lengths, hems, margins, inverted layouts and linear rating.

questions.q: The linear rating of a sheet is
options: The cut length along the roll, in metres per piece
The width of the fabric in metres
Its weight in grams per piece
questions.explain: Linear rating is the length of fabric consumed along the roll for one piece, expressed in metres; it is a fabric consumption figure, not a size.

questions.q: Cutting a sheet 'inverted' means
options: Cutting two sheets from one length
Cutting it across the fabric width, so the cut length along the roll is the finished width plus side margins
questions.explain: When the fabric is wide enough to take the sheet's length across the width, the sheet is turned: its finished width (plus margins) becomes the length taken off the roll.

questions.q: Hems are added to the top and bottom of a flat sheet, while margins are added at the sides.
questions.explain: The lecture describes hems top and bottom and margins on the sides; the hems are wider (the top hem of a sheet is the visible turned-back part).

questions.q: The final rating used in costing is
options: The linear rating plus a wastage allowance
questions.explain: Final rating = linear rating × (1 + wastage). For the single sheet, 1.81 m becomes 1.901 m.

questions.q: To convert a cut length in inches into metres you
questions.explain: There are 39.37 inches in a metre. Dividing by 36 gives yards, and 2.54 converts inches to centimetres.

questions.q: The linear rating is rounded down to the nearest centimetre so that the mill never over-buys fabric.
questions.explain: It is rounded up to the next centimetre (two decimals of a metre): 71.08 in ÷ 39.37 = 1.8054 m is recorded as 1.81 m. Rounding down would leave the cut short.

questions.q: For an inverted flat sheet the fabric width must be at least
options: The finished length plus the top and bottom hems
The cut length along the roll
The finished width plus side margins
questions.explain: In the inverted layout the sheet's length (with its hems) lies across the fabric, so the fabric must be at least that wide; otherwise the sheet must run along the roll.

questions.q: The pillow case row is labelled '3 across'. This means
options: Each pillow case uses three cut lengths
The pillow case is folded three times
Three pillow cases are cut side by side across the fabric width from one cut length
questions.explain: One cut length of 62.80 in yields three pillow cases across the width, so the rating per piece is the cut length in metres divided by three.

questions.q: Which items in the worksheets have a pocket or flap allowance?
questions.explain: Fitted sheets need a pocket to go round the mattress and a U-shape pillow case needs a flap; flat sheets have only hems and margins.

questions.q: The wastage allowance added to the linear rating covers
options: Cutting loss, fabric faults and unusable end pieces
Shrinkage in the customer's wash only
questions.explain: Hems are already inside the cut length; wastage is the extra fabric lost in laying, cutting, faults and roll ends, which costing must still pay for.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The cut-length rules, the 39.37 conversion, rounding up and wastage, and which dimensions actually change the rating.

questions.q: For a flat sheet that runs along the roll (not inverted), the cut length is
options: Finished length + top hem + bottom hem
questions.explain: Along the roll the sheet's length is taken off the roll with its two hems; the width and side margins lie across the fabric and do not consume length.

questions.q: For an inverted flat sheet the cut length along the roll is
questions.explain: The lecture states it directly: inverted cut length = finished width plus side margins. The single sheet: 70.08 + 1.00 = 71.08 in.

questions.q: To convert a finished size in centimetres to inches, you
questions.explain: 178 cm ÷ 2.54 = 70.08 in. Multiplying by 2.54 goes the other way; dividing by 39.37 would turn centimetres into a meaningless small number.

questions.q: Making a non-inverted flat sheet wider (within the fabric width) changes its linear rating.
questions.explain: Width lies across the roll, so only the length plus hems is taken off the roll. The 5 ft (275 cm wide) and 6 ft (310 cm wide) sheets differ in rating only because their lengths differ.

questions.q: A cut length converts to 1.8054 m. The linear rating recorded is
questions.explain: Round up to the next centimetre: 1.81 m. 1.80 is rounding down; 1.90 adds the wastage, which comes later.

questions.q: With wastage w expressed as a fraction, the final rating is
questions.explain: The sheet multiplies: 1.81 × 1.05 = 1.9005 ≈ 1.901 m for the single sheet. Adding w as a bare number would add metres, not a percentage.

questions.q: In the fitted-sheet table the cut length along the roll is the finished width plus the pocket allowance on both sides plus margins.
questions.explain: Every fitted row is finished width in inches + 21 in: single fitted 35.83 + 21 = 56.83 in. The pocket wraps the mattress on both sides, so it is added twice.

questions.q: A linear rating of 2.92 m with 5% wastage gives a final rating of
questions.explain: 2.92 × 1.05 = 3.066 m, the double sheet's figure. 2.97 adds 0.05 m instead of 5%.

questions.q: If a wider fabric allowed 6 pillow cases across instead of 3, with the same cut length, the rating per pillow case would
questions.explain: Rating per piece = cut length in metres ÷ pieces across; twice the pieces from the same length halves the fabric per piece.

questions.q: If the single sheet (178 × 260 cm) were cut along the roll instead of inverted, its cut length would be longer.
questions.explain: Along the roll: 260 cm = 102.36 in plus hems (12.25 in in the sheet) = 114.61 in, against 71.08 in inverted. The inverted layout saves over 40 inches per sheet.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Convert sizes, build cut lengths, round up to linear ratings and add wastage for sheets, fitted sheets and pillow cases.

questions.q: Convert a finished width of 178 cm to inches, to two decimals.
The single sheet is cut inverted: finished width 70.08 in plus a side margin of 0.5 in on each side. Cut length along the roll, in inches?
questions.explain: 70.08 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 71.08 in, the worksheet's figure.

questions.q: Cut length 71.08 in. Linear rating in metres, rounded up to the next centimetre?
Linear rating 1.81 m with 5% wastage. Final rating in metres, to three decimals?
The double sheet (228 × 260 cm) runs along the roll with top and bottom hems totalling 12.25 in. Cut length in inches, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 260 ÷ 2.54 = 102.36 in; + 12.25 = 114.61 in. The 228 cm width lies across the roll and does not enter.

questions.q: Cut length 114.61 in gives a linear rating of 2.92 m after rounding up. Final rating with 5% wastage, to three decimals?
The double fitted sheet is 137 cm wide; the pocket allowances and margins add 21 in. Cut length in inches, to two decimals?
Pillow cases, 3 across: cut length 62.80 in. Convert to metres, round up to the next centimetre, then divide by 3. Rating per pillow case, to three decimals?
A new 200 × 280 cm sheet is cut along the roll with hems totalling 12.25 in. Its linear rating (rounded up) is
questions.explain: 280 ÷ 2.54 = 110.24 in; + 12.25 = 122.49 in; ÷ 39.37 = 3.111 → rounded up to 3.12 m. 3.11 rounds down; 2.80 forgets the hems and the conversion.

questions.q: An order of 5,000 double sheets at a final rating of 3.066 m needs
questions.explain: 5,000 × 3.066 = 15,330 m. 14,600 m uses the linear rating 2.92 without wastage and would run short.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Cutting-room and costing-office situations: layouts, hem changes, actual versus rated consumption.

questions.q: A fabric is 254 cm wide. Can a sheet with a finished length of 260 cm be cut inverted?
options: Yes, 260 cm fits once the hems are folded
No; the finished length plus hems exceeds the fabric width, so it must run along the roll
Yes, if the side margins are removed
Only if the sheet is fitted
questions.explain: Inverted cutting needs the fabric at least as wide as the finished length plus hems; 260 cm already exceeds 254 cm before any hem is added.

questions.q: Why does the inverted layout save fabric for the single sheet?
options: Because width plus margins (71.08 in) is much less than length plus hems (114.61 in)
Because two sheets fit across the roll
questions.explain: The shorter dimension is taken off the roll, so each sheet consumes 1.81 m instead of 2.92 m — provided the fabric is wide enough.

questions.q: The cutting room reports actual consumption of 3.20 m per double sheet against a final rating of 3.066 m. The most likely explanation is
options: The rating was rounded up twice
Wastage in laying, faults and roll ends exceeded the 5% allowance
questions.explain: 3.20 ÷ 2.92 = 1.096, almost 10% over the linear rating. Rounding up contributes less than a centimetre; the gap is real wastage that costing should review.

questions.q: A clerk who buys fabric on the linear rating (1.81 m per single sheet) rather than the final rating will run short.
questions.explain: The linear rating has no allowance for cutting loss or faults; 1,000 sheets need 1,901 m, not 1,810 m.

questions.q: An order of 2,400 single fitted sheets at a final rating of 1.523 m. Fabric required, to the nearest metre?
Fabric costs Rs 310 per metre and the single sheet's final rating is 1.901 m. Fabric cost per sheet is
questions.explain: 1.901 × 310 = Rs 589.31. Rs 561.10 uses the linear rating 1.81 and misses the wastage.

questions.q: A buyer asks for a bottom hem 2 in deeper on the double sheet, which runs along the roll. The linear rating changes by about
questions.explain: 2 in ÷ 39.37 = 0.051 m more taken off the roll for every sheet, before rounding. 0.02 confuses inches with centimetres.

questions.q: The same 2 in deeper bottom hem is requested on the single sheet, which is cut inverted. The linear rating
options: Does not change, because hems lie across the roll in the inverted layout
questions.explain: Inverted cut length = finished width + side margins; the hems add to the dimension across the fabric. It only matters if the fabric is still wide enough.

questions.q: For the 76 × 48 cm pillow case cut 3 across, the minimum fabric width is roughly
questions.explain: The 76 cm length runs along the roll (doubled in the U-shape cut), so the 48 cm width is what sits across the fabric, three times over.

questions.q: The wastage percentage should be applied to the cut length before it is rounded up to the next centimetre.
questions.explain: The sheet rounds first (1.8054 → 1.81) and then multiplies by 1.05 (→ 1.901). Doing it the other way gives a slightly different, non-standard figure.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder cases: comparing layouts, inverting the arithmetic, and the slips in units and rounding that distort a rating.

questions.q: The 6 ft sheet is 310 × 270 cm. If it were cut inverted with 0.5 in margins each side, its linear rating in metres (rounded up to the next centimetre) would be
For that 6 ft sheet the worksheet's along-the-roll rating is 3.02 m. Which layout uses less fabric, and why?
options: Along the roll, because this sheet's width (310 cm) is greater than its length (270 cm)
Inverted, because it has no hems
Inverted, because inverted always saves fabric
questions.explain: Inverting puts the width on the roll; when the width is the larger dimension, that costs more fabric (3.13 m) than running the 270 cm length with hems (3.02 m).

questions.q: Final ratings at 5% wastage are 3.287 m inverted and 3.171 m along the roll. For 10,000 sheets, how many more metres does the inverted layout need?
questions.explain: 0.116 m × 10,000 = 1,160 m of extra fabric.

questions.q: A student converts the double sheet's 114.61 in cut length by dividing by 36 and records 3.18 m. The error is
options: Dividing by inches per yard instead of inches per metre (39.37)
questions.explain: 114.61 ÷ 36 = 3.18 yards, not metres; 114.61 ÷ 39.37 = 2.911 → 2.92 m. The 9% overstatement would be passed into every quotation.

questions.q: A cut length converts to exactly 2.9100 m. The linear rating recorded is
questions.explain: Rounding up to the next centimetre changes nothing when the value is already a whole number of centimetres; 2.92 would add an unnecessary centimetre.

questions.q: On a narrower fabric only 2 pillow cases fit across. With the same cut length (1.60 m after rounding), the rating per pillow case is
questions.explain: 1.60 ÷ 2 = 0.80 m, half as much again as the 0.533 m achieved with 3 across.

questions.q: For the pillow case the rounding up is applied to the full cut length in metres before dividing by 3, which is why the per-piece rating 0.533 can have three decimals.
questions.explain: 62.80 in → 1.5951 → 1.60 m, then ÷ 3 = 0.5333 m; the 1.60 is the figure actually cut, so it is the one rounded.

questions.q: The 5 ft fitted sheet is 152 cm wide. If the pocket and margin allowance is raised from 21 in to 23 in, the new cut length in inches is
That new cut length of 82.84 in gives a linear rating of
questions.explain: 82.84 ÷ 39.37 = 2.1042 m, rounded up to 2.11 m. 2.10 rounds down; 2.21 is a slip of a decimal in the division.

questions.q: The 6 ft fitted sheet has a final rating of 2.489 m. At Rs 280 per metre, the fabric cost of 1,000 sheets is
questions.explain: 2.489 × 280 × 1,000 = Rs 696,920. Rs 663,600 uses the linear rating 2.37 m and leaves out the wastage.
